articles.title: Use of treated water for non-drinking purposes in govt offices; supply it to data centres: Telangana CM
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy has directed officials to ensure the use of treated wastewater for all non-drinking purposes in government offices and public spaces, and called for strict monitoring of sewage treatment plants (STPs) to maintain water quality and prevent the wastage of potable water.

At a review meeting on STPs and treated water, held at the MCR HRD Institute in Hyderabad on Wednesday (October 28, 2026), the Chief Minister called for the use of artificial intelligence (AI) technology at the treatment plants and directed officials to appoint a special officer at every plant. He also asked them to connect all the plants to the Command Control Centre and ensure monitoring by the Hyderabad Disaster Response and Assets Protection Agency (HYDRAA).

Mr. Reddy said treated water should be used for landscaping along the Outer Ring Road (ORR) and in other areas. The use of treated water should also be made mandatory for landscaping at the Secretariat and the Chief Minister’s Office, as well as at public parks.

Directing officials to issue orders making the use of treated water compulsory for non-potable purposes in government offices, he said the Railways and Hyderabad Metro Rail should also be brought under the initiative. It should be ensured that treated water is used for all eligible purposes instead of fresh drinking water, he said. Treated water has to be used at public parks and for cleaning roads.

Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy at a meeting with officials on usage of treated water from sewage treatment plants (STP), in Hyderabad on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) | Photo Credit: BY ARRANGEMENT

The Chief Minister wanted treated water tankers to be tracked to monitor their movement and use. He also called for a toll-free number to facilitate the supply of treated water and asked officials to undertake a wide publicity campaign to promote its use.

He directed officials to incorporate conditions mandating the use of treated water at the stage of granting building permissions. Private sewage treatment plants should be encouraged, while the feasibility of operating treatment plants using solar power should be examined, he said.
The Chief Minister also asked officials to ensure the supply of treated water to data centres , given their requirements, and to take measures keeping future demand in view.

Stressing that water quality should not be compromised under any circumstances, Mr. Reddy said the government must ensure that Hyderabad did not face a shortage of drinking water. He called for continuous monitoring of drinking water supply and cautioned officials against negligence.

The departments concerned were directed to ensure that the measures announced at the meeting were implemented from November 1. HMWSSB officials said that currently, treated water from 26 STPs is being supplied through green tankers, providing the resource free of cost. Only transportation charges are collected from consumers.

Chief Secretary Sanjay Jaju, Secretary to the Chief Minister Manick Raj, Director of School Education Naveen Nicholas, Cyberabad Municipal Commissioner Srujana, Malkajgiri Municipal Commissioner Vinay Krishna Reddy, Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board Managing Director Ashok Reddy, TGSPDCL Managing Director Jitesh V. Patil were among the officials present at the meeting.

articles.title: Cyclone Arnab LIVE: Amit Shah speaks with CMs of affected States, assures all support
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A new low-pressure area formed over the south Andaman Sea on Thursday morning, a day after Cyclone Arnab crossed the coast. The IMD expects it to strengthen and become a depression over the southeast Bay of Bengal by October 31. Officials in Amaravati said it would “most likely” affect Andhra Pradesh.
Arnab itself has weakened into a depression over south Chhattisgarh and south Odisha and is expected to fade further by Thursday evening.
A fresh low-pressure area has formed over the Andaman Sea days after Cyclone Arnab and could become a depression by October 31, says IMD Amaravati.

Floodwater from an overflowing rivulet rose above the danger mark at a railway bridge between Ichchapuram and Jhadupudi on Thursday morning. The Brahmapur-Visakhapatnam passenger and express trains and the Visakhapatnam-Brahmapur passenger have been cancelled. Several long-distance trains, including the Falaknuma Express to Howrah, are being diverted via Vizianagaram and Titlagarh, skipping Srikakulam Road, Palasa and Bhubaneswar.
Floodwater at a railway bridge near Ichchapuram has led to the cancellation of three Brahmapur-Visakhapatnam trains; long-distance trains are diverted.

The Nagavali at Srikakulam was just 1 cm below its warning level at noon on Thursday and still rising, Water Resources Department data showed. Rivers across Srikakulam, Vizianagaram and Parvathipuram Manyam districts kept swelling though the skies had cleared. The Bahuda, fed by water released from a dam in Odisha, sent floodwater into the border town of Ichchapuram.
Rivers in Srikakulam, Vizianagaram and Parvathipuram Manyam swelled after Cyclone Arnab, flooding Ichchapuram; a lineman died during repairs in Vizianagaram.

Rain and squally winds lashed parts of West Bengal on Thursday (October 29, 2026) as the “very severe” cyclonic storm Arnab weakened into a depression and lay centred over south Chhattisgarh and adjoining south Odisha.

According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), the depression is likely to weaken to a well-marked low pressure by Thursday evening (October 29, 2026), bringing heavy rain in West Bengal till Friday (October 30, 2026).

It also noted that a fresh low pressure formed over the South Andaman Sea on Thursday morning. The weather system is likely to intensify into a depression over the southwest Bay of Bengal as it moves in a west-northwestward direction, the weather office said.

Union Home Minister Amit Shah spoke with the Chief Ministers of Andhra Pradesh, Puducherry, Odisha and Chhattisgarh in the wake of Cyclone Arnab, and assured all assistance to mitigate the hardships of the people.
“It is very likely to move north-northwestwards during the next 48 hours and weaken gradually. It will weaken into a deep depression by midnight of October 28, 2026,” the IMD said.

articles.title: Social media users trash Telangana CEO’s claims on SIR, call the process a sham
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Chief Electoral Officer C. Sudharsan Reddy faced public backlash after he posted online that the procedure and guidelines of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls were duly followed in Telangana. Some social media users even threatened to move court over the deletion of voters’ names.

In a post on his official X account, the CEO said enumeration forms had been distributed to all electors and collected after being filled in. The draft electoral rolls were then prepared, excluding the names of electors whose forms had not been received.

“This was done only after House-to-House visit and due enquiry by BLOs and not done unilaterally. Also opportunity has been given to left out Electors during the period of Claims and Objections for filing their claims if any (sic),” Mr. Reddy posted, tagging the Election Commission of India’s spokesperson.

He added that special camps were held on October 15 and 16 to give electors another opportunity to ensure that all eligible voters were included and ineligible names excluded from the rolls. He maintained that the prescribed procedures had been followed throughout the process.

However, several social media users disputed the CEO’s claim that Booth Level Officers (BLOs) had conducted house-to-house visits, while others complained that they had not received enumeration forms.

“No proper procedure was followed by @CEO_Telangana. EFs were distributed but never collected. BLO’s phone was unreachable, officials refused to accept forms directly at offices. Ultimately, my name was deleted. Now, was I marked as duplicate voter, absent/shifted, or deceased?” questioned Sharath Raj, a user on X.

Sameer Mathad, a software developer, posted that he was in the process of filing [a case]. His name was deleted, and no BLO visited his home. Calling the process a sham in Telangana, he said the BLO gave the forms to a local leader who never contacted him.

Syed Irfan, an activist, called the CEO’s statement ‘purest form of lie’, and said he too had not received his enumeration form. “Jhoot aisa bolo jispe yaqeen kiya jaa sake [A lie should be believable]. “Distributed to All” is the biggest lie. Shame on you,” he posted as a reply.
Sitaram Dhulipala, another user, pointed out that voters of a single household were dispersed in different polling stations, and that house-to-house visits were not conducted.

“House-to-House visit? Is this some kind of joke to you? No one ever visited my apartment or my colony, and you people blatantly say House-to-House visit. No, you did not follow the process correctly. Stop lying! (sic),” said a user called Saiekrishna.

Rajesh, another user, invited the CEO to court. Tagging ECI, and Supreme Court, he challenged the CEO to prove that BLO had visited his home. “My name has been removed from the rolls without giving any reason, even when I submitted the SIR form and I am still alive. How can you say only dead have been deleted?,” wrote P.Jyothiswaroop, quoting the CEO’s post.
Deva Raj, also an X user, threatened to go to court if a BLO does not visit his home and follow due procedure as claimed by the CEO.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: Deva Raj, also an X user, threatened to go to court if a BLO does not visit his home and follow due procedure as claimed by the CEO.

articles.title: Low pressure forms in Andaman Sea after Cyclone Arnab, may affect Andhra Pradesh
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A day after Cyclone Arnab crossed the Andhra Pradesh coast , a fresh low-pressure area has formed over the south Andaman Sea, and India Meteorological Department (IMD) officials say it could affect the State.

According to the latest information from the IMD, Amaravati, a low-pressure area formed over the south Andaman Sea at around 5.30 a.m. on Thursday (October 29, 2026), under the influence of a cyclonic circulation. It was still over the same region at 8.30 a.m.

(A). Depression over south Chhattisgarh and adjoining south Odisha The Depression (Remnant of Very Severe Cyclonic Storm "Arnab") over south Chhattisgarh and adjoining south Odisha moved nearly northwards with the speed of 18 kmph during past 6 hours, and lay centered at 0830 hrs IST of today, the 29th October, over the same region near latitude 19.4°N and longitude 81.9°E, about 40 km north-northwest of Jagdalpur (Chhattisgarh), 180 km southwest of Titlagarh (Odisha), 150 km west-southwest of Bhawanipatna (Odisha), 200 km south of Raipur (Odisha), and 310 km southwest of Sambalpur (Odisha). It is very likely to continue to move nearly northwards, and weaken into a well marked low pressure area over North Chhattisgarh and adjoining Northwest Odisha around evening of today, the 29th October 2026. During past 24 hours ending at 0830 hours IST of today, there has been widespread rainfall activity over north Andhra Pradesh, Northeast Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand, and Gangetic West Bengal with heavy to very heavy rainfall at a few places and extremely heavy rainfall (21 cm or more) at a isolated places over South Odisha and North Andhra Pradesh, heavy to very heavy rainfall at isolated places over North Odisha and heavy rainfall at isolated places over Northeast Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, and Gangetic West Bengal. Exceptional heavy rainfall occurred over south Odisha during past 24 hours ending at 0830 IST of today. The highest rainfall of 546 mm occurred over Patrapur (dist Ganjam) followed by 503 mm over Sorada (dist Ganjam), 462 mm over G.Udaygiri (Kandhamal), 458 mm over Mahendragarh (Gajapati), 388 mm over Sanakhemundi (Ganjam), 309 mm over Chikiti (Ganjam). The system is under continuous surveillance of the Doppler Weather Radar at Raipur and Sambalpur. (B) Low Pressure Area over South Andaman Sea and neighborhood. The low pressure area over south Andaman Sea & neighbourhood persisted over the same region at 0830 Hrs IST of today, the 29th October 2026. It is very likely to move west-northwestwards and become a Well Marked Low Pressure Area over south Andaman Sea and adjoining Andaman & Nicobar Islands during next 24 hours. Thereafter, continuing to move west-northwestwards, it is very likely to concentrate into a depression over southeast Bay of Bengal and adjoining Andaman Nicobar & Islands and Andaman Sea during subsequent 24 hours.

It is very likely to move west-northwestwards and become a well-marked low-pressure area over the south Andaman Sea and adjoining Andaman and Nicobar Islands by Friday (October 30). It is then likely to keep moving west-northwest and concentrate into a depression over the southeast Bay of Bengal and adjoining areas of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands by October 31. Officials of the IMD in Amaravati said it would “most likely” affect Andhra Pradesh. They are watching to see whether the system intensifies further.

The IMD has already forecast heavy rain at isolated places in coastal Andhra Pradesh on November 1, 2 and 3. November 1 is polling day for the urban local body elections, which the State Election Commission has decided to hold as scheduled.

The remnant of Arnab has moved inland and weakened. At 8.30 a.m. on Thursday it was a depression about 40 km north-northwest of Jagdalpur in Chhattisgarh, moving north at 18 kmph. It is expected to weaken further into a well-marked low-pressure area over north Chhattisgarh and northwest Odisha by Thursday evening.

The storm’s remnant dumped exceptional rain on south Odisha in the 24 hours to 8.30 a.m. on Thursday. Patrapur in Ganjam district, where the Baghalati dam is located, recorded 546 mm, the highest. Sorada in Ganjam got 503 mm and Mahendragarh in Gajapati 458 mm. Water released from the Baghalati dam has flooded Ichchapuram and nearby villages on the Andhra Pradesh side of the border.

articles.title: Telangana SIR: Form-6 rejections and Form-7 deletions unusually high during pre-SIR period
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: There is a high likelihood of a large number of genuine electors being kept out of the final rolls after the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of Electoral Rolls in Telangana. They constitute not only the voters excluded from the draft electoral rolls and those deleted during Claims & Objections phase but also applicants whose Form-6 were rejected.
The number of rejections constitutes close to 27% of the total Form-6 applications processed during Pre-SIR and SIR phases, which is very high.

A total of 10,77,450 Form-6 applications were received from 119 constituencies across Telangana, of which, 5,20,331 were received during the six month pre-SIR phase between January 1, 2026, and June 14, 2026. During the Enumeration Phase and before publication of draft electoral rolls, between June 15, 2026, and August 16, 2026, a total 3,18,042 applications were received for new voter registration.

The number of Form-6 applications received during Claims & Objections phase, when the Election Commission of India (ECI) publicised and exhorted the new and deleted voters to get themselves registered, was only 1,70,374. Post the Claims & Objections period which ended on October 7, 2026, till October 28, 2026, a total 68,703 Form-6 applications were received.

Of all these applications, a total 2,43,643 were rejected, as per the information shared from the office of the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO). This is close to 23%, calculated on the total number of applications received. Considering that a total 1,61,214 applications are still pending verification, the rejection rate climbs to 27%, which is unusual.
Majority of these rejections were made during the pre-SIR phase. Of the 5,20,331 applications received during this phase, a total 1,92,574 were rejected, which amounts to 37% rejection rate.
Together with the total deletions effected during the pre-SIR and SIR phases, the exclusions from the electoral roll could be well over 80 lakh.

The number of voters excluded during the Enumeration Phase constitutes the largest chunk of the total deletions, at 73,39,235. Over 4.54 lakh voters were deleted through filing of Form-7 even before the SIR exercise began. Official records show that during the six month period between January 1, 2026 and June 14, 2026, a total 5,13,375 Form-7 applications were filed for deletion of names from rolls or objecting to the inclusion of names. Of these, 4,54,340 were accepted.

While officials claim that they were Demographically Similar Entries and Photo Similar Entries sifted by an application on the ECINET software, no explanation was given for 47,303 Form-7 applications which were rejected during the same period.

On the whole, starting from January 1, 2026, a total 5,81,273 Form-7 applications were filed, of which, 5,08,057 were accepted. These include the electors found ineligible for final roll during notice period. Only 54,681 Form-7 applications were rejected, and 18,535 are under process.

Of the 50,502 electors found ineligible for final rolls, 19,535 were rejected citing logical discrepancies, and 30,207 for not mapping themselves with 2002 SIR rolls. A total 2,58,04,484 electors have been parked for final publication, including 89,63,065 electors who were served notices. Electors for whom hearing is still pending or who are yet to be served notices number over a lakh.

articles.title: PM questions Congress over party’s MLC election results
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) took a dig at the Congress, pointing out that the principal Opposition party failed to win a single seat in the Member of Legislative Council (MLC) elections held using ballot papers across four major States.
“MLC elections in 28 seats across four big States — Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar and Karnataka. Elections held using ballot papers. Guess how many seats Congress won?” said Mr. Modi on X.

At the time of filing the story, results for eight seats had been declared in Uttar Pradesh. While the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) won five seats, the Samajwadi Party secured three. In Bihar, the BJP-led NDA alliance was close to winning four seats. The Jan Suraaj Party opened its account with one seat, while the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) also secured one seat and Independents bagged two. In Karnataka, the BJP-JD(S) alliance swept all four seats. The Maharashtra Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) had not declared the results for the five MLC constituencies.

Earlier, at a press briefing, BJP MP and spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi said the MLC election results showed a lack of public support for the Congress party and that its methods were not working. He said the ambitions of Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and the Congress to “spread anarchy by creating a whirlwind of lies” appeared to have been dented by the results.
MLC elections in 28 seats across 4 big states - Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar and Karnataka. Elections held using ballot papers. Guess how many seats Congress won? 🧐

“The most important aspect of these elections is that they were conducted through ballot papers and ballot boxes... This makes it clear that the Congress party lacks the ability to secure the support of the public or the concerned electorate in any kind of election, whether conducted using EVMs (Electronic Voting Machines) or through ballot papers and ballot boxes,” he said.

“The Congress party should understand that after spending nearly two weeks sightseeing and enjoying himself, Rahul Gandhi has now returned in all his pomp and glory, talking about launching a movement to create problems for the Indian economy. He should understand that neither the public nor the MLAs are with him,” Mr. Trivedi said.

He said that while BJP president Nitin Nabin was touring Uttar Pradesh and Union Home Minister Amit Shah was in Punjab, Mr. Gandhi was “travelling around” Vietnam. The problem lay neither with EVMs nor with voter lists or ballot papers, but “in the delusions entrenched in their minds and their (Congress’s) habit of not working”, said Mr. Trivedi.

On the Keralam Congress’s unconditional apology to the Supreme Court, he described its now-deleted social media post on X about the Chief Justice of India as “highly objectionable, disgraceful and vulgar”.

Responding to the Prime Minister’s post, Congress leader Pawan Khera said Mr. Modi should demonstrate his confidence in the BJP’s electoral prowess by committing to hold all future Lok Sabha and Assembly elections through ballot paper, suspend the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, restore the 13.3 crore deleted voters, remove Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and repeal the law granting him lifelong immunity.
“Until Modi acts on these demands, his claims are nothing but hogwash — hollow words no one can take seriously,” Mr. Khera said.

articles.title: Disinvestment as key economic strategy
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: S even months into 2026-27, the fiscal year has been shaped by global uncertainty, high energy prices and worries over a deficient monsoon. Against this backdrop, disinvestment and asset monetisation have helped in navigating a challenging fiscal year. While receipts were already on course to meet the budget target, the government’s approval of the sale of its share in the IDBI Bank on October 14 makes it likely that the target will be exceeded. For the industry and investors, the receipts are a signal of the government’s continued commitment to reforms and a larger role for the private sector. This year so far, the disinvestment trajectory has progressed well, even before the IDBI stake sale. According to DIPAM data, the Centre mobilised ₹62,124 crore in April-September 2026 through disinvestment and asset monetisation, of which ₹55,757 crore came from disinvestment. These collections had already reached 78% of the full-year budget target of ₹80,000 crore. With the IDBI proceeds, the collections are to head past the target.

This comes at a time when the government looks to diversify its revenue sources amid rising expenditure commitments. Net tax revenue rose by a modest 3.4% in April-August 2026 and non-tax revenue by 3.2%, while capital expenditure was up by over 18%. Overall, the fiscal deficit has already reached 42% of the budgeted levels which implies a tight balance between revenue shortfalls and spending risks.

However, disinvestment should not be seen merely as a tool for meeting fiscal targets. It is a policy choice aimed at unlocking greater value from public assets, widening public ownership, and improving efficiency and governance through greater market discipline. The 2022 LIC IPO which drew in many first-time retail investors and policyholders remains a prime example.

This was precisely the rationale behind the government’s 2021 New Public Sector Enterprise (PSE) Policy which envisages a “bare minimum presence” of PSEs in strategic sectors. Likewise, the National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP) re-engines capital via mature public assets. A target of ₹16.72 lakh crore has been set under NMP 2.0 for FY26-30 after having achieved 90% of its Phase 1 goal.

This year, however, until this month, receipts had come mainly through Offer for Sale (OFS) measures which help to broaden ownership but keep the status quo on an enterprise’s operations. The strategic sale of the IDBI Bank since Air India in 2022 is an encouraging sign. From an industry perspective, the IDBI sale is more than a one-off sale. It is one of the largest Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) deals in India’s financial sector and constitutes as the first step towards a ‘Privatisation 2.0’ framework. More importantly, this framework is premised on being investor-led, professionally managed and time-bound. Two changes would help to turn into a template.

First, the selection criteria for disinvestments of PSEs should move to a demand-based approach instead of being led by the government. It would work better to first gauge interest across a wider pool and prioritise PSEs that draw strong bids at expected valuations, with structured investor feedback flagging procedural and regulatory hurdles early. Second, a rolling three-year privatisation stream, based on investor interest and the government’s strategic priorities, would give investors time for due diligence, which means deeper participation and better price discovery.

Given the fact that privatisation of several PSEs is a long journey, calibrated disinvestment could serve as an interim measure. CII analysis suggests that bringing the government’s stake down to 51% across 95 listed PSEs could fetch about ₹9 lakh crore, with the government remaining the single largest shareholder. PSEs where the government holds 75% or less could be taken up in the first two years, followed by those with higher government holdings. A dedicated body, with a ministerial board, industry experts as advisers and a management team, could steer the process.

To be sure, none of the above makes a case for fiscal complacency. Deficits and public debt tend to rise in uncertain times and stay elevated long after the shock subsides. Staying on the path of fiscal prudence is essential to ensure that the government can continue investing in health and education without crowding out private investment.

Amidst various global headwinds, a healthy progress on disinvestments with more big-ticket sales such as the IDBI will provide the Centre the required cushion to stay on course with fiscal consolidation.
Chandrajit Banerjee is Director General, Confederation of Indian Industry

articles.title: U.S. Fed holds interest rates steady despite surging inflation
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The US Federal Reserve on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) held interest rates steady, in line with market expectations, days ahead of crucial midterm elections where surging inflation has been a key issue.

The 12-member Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to hold rates at a target range between 3.75 and 4.00%, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation, after having hiked for the first time in three years at its previous meeting in September.

“The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s two percent goal,” the Fed said in a statement announcing its decision.
Two members of the committee, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, dissented, calling instead for an immediate 0.25-percentage-point rate hike.
The central bank has missed its long-term two-percent target for inflation for more than five years, with households and businesses battered by sustained price increases.

U.S. President Donald Trump's war on Iran, launched in late February, has sent energy prices skyrocketing and fueled domestic inflation, alongside his wide-ranging tariff policies. Prices have also been driven by an investment boom in artificial intelligence (AI) technology and the build-out of huge data centres to support it. The decision comes six days ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, in which the Democratic Party is seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress from Mr. Trump's Republicans. Mr. Trump's handling of the economy has been a key issue throughout the campaign, with working-class households across the country struggling to make ends meet despite largely stable overall economic growth.
U.S. consumer inflation came in hotter than expected in September, clocking in at 3.7%, edging back towards a three-year high established in May.
Still, key policymakers at the Fed -- including Mr. Warsh -- have signalled that they did not see an urgency to raise rates again immediately.

Speaking in Bangkok earlier this month, Mr. Warsh said that U.S. economic conditions had “broadly conformed” to policymakers’ expectations, fueling speculation that the Fed may pause at the October meeting.
On Wednesday (October 28, 2026), the Fed said economic activity in the United States was expanding at a “strong” pace, upgrading its language from the FOMC meeting six weeks prior.

Wendy Edelberg, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told AFP before the meeting that a decision to hold after raising rates in September was potentially contradictory, given the labour market -- the Fed’s other mandate -- has been largely stable.
“In terms of the economics of it, I don’t totally understand the logic,” she said.

articles.title: How neoliberalism turned the world against its young
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: France is in turmoil. And Albania. And Spain. Even India. As were Bangladesh or Sri Lanka earlier. The list goes on. While the specific demands may vary, one thing is common across these mobilisations: the young are on the streets. Why are the young angry the world over? In this piece, we look at the first world, in particular the G7 bloc, to understand why indeed.
France is a good example to understand what is happening in the global North. Emmanuel Macron, the antagonist according to the students in the French protests, has been in power since May 14, 2017.

Over his almost a decade-long reign, France has witnessed severe economic problems — high unemployment, low growth, rising cost of living, falling real wages and severe cutbacks in public expenditure. It is not a happenstance, therefore, that the spark that lit this protest was the lack of resources and staff at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in Créteil (a suburb of Paris).

At the heart of it all is the neoliberal economic model, which aggressively enforced reduced public expenditure in general, and welfare spending in particular. Whether it’s Macron in France or Biden/Clinton in the U.S. or Starmer in the U.K., those championing this economic model have either been ousted or are on the brink of losing power.

The system has angered young people in particular. Although overall unemployment rates have remained high since the pandemic, youth unemployment rates in G7 countries are now almost twice as high, if not higher (Chart 1). Generation Z (Gen Z), which has taken to the streets, comprises those born between 1997 and 2012, putting them in the 14-29 age group today. That cohort overlaps with the age group 15-29 shown in the chart.

As is well known, unlike countries in the Global South, developed countries are ageing societies, with the share of young people in their populations declining over time. Yet, as their relative population share shrinks, youth unemployment continues to rise. While fewer young people enter the labour force each year, many more join the ranks of the unemployed. Clearly, the problem is not an excess supply of labour but a lack of demand for it.

As is the case with most economics questions, this also has broadly two sides — orthodox and heterodox. The orthodox side believes unemployment has to do with high rigid wages, inflexible labour markets, lack of a skilled labour force, most of which puts the blame, directly or indirectly, on the working class itself for its misfortune.
The heterodox side, in sharp contrast, argues it is the decision of the capitalist class to employ or not to employ workers which determines unemployment in the economy.

Consider a typical labour market — demand for labour comes from the capitalists; supply of it comes from the workers. Capitalists would like to employ as many as they could to maximise their profits. The lower the wage rate, the higher the profits, and so the demand for labour rises as wages fall (downward-sloping demand curve in graph 1). The supply curve, on the other hand, is upward sloping because as the wages rise, more workers join the labour force. The intersection of the two (point E) represents full employment — those who seek work at that wage get it.

When the economy gets stuck at point A — demand for labour (point A) is less than its supply (point B) — the economy has involuntary unemployment (equal to the gap AB). But what stops the economy from reaching point E?

Orthodox economics would tell us the wages are way too high, for which either the labour unions or rigid labour market legislation (against ‘hire and fire’, for example) are responsible. To be sure, there are other theories like the ‘efficiency wages’ which explain why the economy remains stuck at A.

The heterodox approaches argue that labour demand depends on the level of demand for goods and services in the economy. Demand, under ‘pure’ capitalism, consists of investment and consumption (see (A) in box 1). Let’s assume, for simplicity, workers consume all their wages and capitalists save their entire profits. Consumption demand would then depend on employment (wage bill), so it cannot be the cause of unemployment. The real cause, therefore, is investment. The less the capitalists decide to invest, less will be the total induced demand for goods and services, and the lower will be the need to employ workers.

articles.title: Vedanta Group eyeing $20 billion profits over next two years: Chairman Anil Agarwal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Vedanta Group is targeting revenue of $50 billion and profits of $20 billion over the next two years, founder and chairman Anil Agarwal said at an industry event in Kolkata.
“This year we would be making $30 billion revenue and $11 billion in profits. In two years, we would scale our revenues to $50 billion with $20 billion in profits,” he said.
The privately-owned diversified commodities producer has interests spanning aluminium, zinc, oil and gas, power, iron and steel, copper and other critical minerals.

Separately, its recently listed Vedanta Aluminium reported more than a doubling of net profit year-on-year to ₹6,187 crore for the quarter ended September. Revenue rose 41% to ₹22,066 crore during the period.
The company increased aluminium production by 5% year-on-year to 649 kilotonnes (KT). Production of value-added aluminium products rose 31% to 432 KT, while alumina output climbed 37% to 895 KT.

Vedanta Aluminium also reduced its net debt by ₹3,090 crore during the quarter compared with the preceding quarter, signalling an improvement in its debt position alongside higher production and earnings.

articles.title: The way out of the dangerous trap
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: India, celebrated as the world’s fastest-growing economy, has become the world’s fourth-largest economy, and is expected to be the next engine of global growth. Yet beneath these numbers lies a grim reality: India is drifting toward the middle-income trap, in which countries exhaust their gains from cheap labour and rapid catch-up and fail to transition to an innovation-driven, productivity-based economy. Weak job creation, stagnant wages, sluggish private investment, and low productivity are reinforcing one another, threatening to stall the country’s rise before it reaches high-income status. Many countries in the Global South are caught in this trap. India’s structural crisis is unique and more serious than not just a consequence of wars in West Asia disturbing its supply chain or premature automation from AI.

The signs of distress are visible in the youth protests across the country. Private investment remains sluggish, wage growth is stagnant, and household consumption is weak. Manufacturing has failed to generate enough jobs, while post-pandemic recovery has favoured large corporations and the digital economy, leaving the informal sector barely touched. Jobless growth emerges because productivity gains stay concentrated in narrow, capital- and skill-intensive enclaves that create little employment. This simultaneous rise of rising inequality and low productivity is a dangerous trap.

Economists are typically divided in explaining this trap. Those trained in pro-market orthodoxy argue India needs another set of market reforms — no less than what occurred during the 1991 moment — more labour flexibility, agricultural reform, deregulation, and infrastructure investment. Those on the left and typically in the Keynesian mould argue that the economy suffers from weak aggregate demand and needs more public spending, redistribution and social protection. Both arguments hold a kernel of truth, but miss the larger point: India’s current situation stems not only from supply and demand constraints but from institutions shaped by social norms, which decide both how markets set incentives and prices, and how the State allocates resources and provides public goods.

It is no surprise, then, that both the State and the market operate suboptimally. Private capital, more freer from regulation than ever, does not do well on productivity and innovation. Its competitiveness comes from cutting costs rather than innovating. It couldn’t even absorb knowledge that comes with FDI. It couldn’t increase productivity that results from both inter-sectoral movements and innovation within sectors either. On the other hand, capital is heavily subsidised, lowering its relative price vis-à-vis labour in a labour-surplus economy. India’s innovation is skewed, with R&D spending at a paltry 0.65% of GDP, while technology adoption remains weak and far from spontaneous. Despite the government’s growing size, India’s capacity to intervene — even to provide basic services like health centres or schooling — remains among the lowest anywhere.

The Left–Right debate focuses on the size and quality of government expenditure, but the problem lies elsewhere. The same social norms that shape resource allocation also drive its inefficient use. For instance, India has historically underfunded mass education while subsidising higher education for elites, tilting spending toward the privileged. That same elite bias later drove the service-sector-heavy growth of post-reform India, letting upper castes monopolise better occupations while relegating low-productivity work to others.

India’s social norms are distinctive: they decide how State and market function while producing durable inequality and legitimising it. Having long undermined mass education, India’s vocational training system remains poorly managed and chronically underfunded. Fewer than 3% of the workforce has any formal vocational education. Of roughly 14,000 ITIs offering about 25 lakh seats, actual intake is only about 48%, and even among graduates, the employment rate is just 63% — far below the 90%-plus seen in many other countries.

Societies set up institutions based on their interests and norms. Economists often take self-interest as central to economic motives. Yet social norms determine the kind of institutions that take shape, which in turn decide how individual efforts are channelised into productive activities. These institutions work as the taproot of entrepreneurial success. As this year’s Nobel Prize winner Joel Mokyr has argued, modern growth depends on the accumulation and diffusion of “useful knowledge,” the practical skills that enable societies to innovate, adapt and raise productivity.

For Mokyr, sustained growth rests on the coevolution of science, technology and the spread of useful knowledge, something that failed to take strong root in India. India has historically privileged abstract education over vocational and technical knowledge. University degrees command prestige while technical courses training electricians, welders, machinists and carpenters do not. This hierarchy is not accidental. It reflects centuries of caste-based occupational stratification, where manual and artisanal work has been systematically undervalued despite its indispensable role in industrial development.

The result is a chronic shortage of skilled manufacturing workers even as millions of educated young Indians struggle to find decent jobs. Ironically, India’s Chief Economic Adviser, V Anantha Nageswaran, recently urged the youth to pursue trades such as welding and plumbing instead of chasing software jobs or MBAs.

But it won’t happen unless India changes its social valuation of skills. Take the marriage market: some skills and occupations carry a premium over others. These social valuations shape educational choices, occupational aspirations and ultimately the allocation of labour.

Data show a persistent and steady decline in the labour intensity of production technology across sectors. Even in traditionally labour-intensive sectors, the trend is likely to accelerate with the advent of AI. India therefore needs to recalibrate not just production and distribution, but also their valuation. Without changing the cultural valuation of skills and the way production itself is organised. India may fall into a low-income, low-productivity trap.

Countries that escaped the middle-income trap — from South Korea to China — did not simply build factories but built institutions capable of creating and diffusing useful knowledge across domains. China’s interventions in education and health laid the foundation for its later productive capacity. Its early state-led industrialisation was accompanied by massive investments in technical education, local manufacturing capability and technological learning. By contrast, countries such as Brazil, Argentina, Thailand and the Philippines, which failed to build or sustain such institutions, became stuck in the middle-income trap. Like India, large sections of their populations remain dependent on public transfers and handouts to secure the basic requirements of a prosperous existence.

articles.title: The gap in manufacturing sector GVA
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Early this year, the National Statistical Office (NSO) released the new series of the National Accounts Statistics (NAS). It shows that the manufacturing sector’s gross value added (GVA) is ₹38.6 lakh crore (₹38.6 trillion), constituting 14.7 per cent of GDP (gross domestic product) for the year 2023-24 at current prices. How reliable is the official estimate? This article investigates.

The manufacturing sector has two parts: One comprises all registered factories employing 10+/20+ workers with/without power, including registered companies (defined as the organised/formal sector). The other comprises unincorporated/ informal/ household units consisting of small factories/workshops falling outside the corporate/factory sector. The Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) reports the production accounts of the factory sector, while the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE) covers the informal sector. The combined output (GVA) of the factory and unincorporated sectors almost completely represents total manufacturing output.

For 2023-24, the sum of the GVA of units covered by the ASI and ASUSE is ₹27.4 lakh crore (the Alternative Estimate or, AE). The official figure, as per the NAS, is ₹38.6 lakh crore. It is higher than the AE by a whopping 40.9 per cent. Let’s call this the GAP. What could account for it?

While minor variations between the two estimates is understandable due to methodological or definitional issues, such a substantial GAP between the two estimates using official data sources surely raises many questions.

What are the data sources used for estimating the official GVA? For the unincorporated sector, it is ASUSE – the same as what we have used to estimate the AE. Hence, it cannot account for the GAP noted above. Moreover, the unincorporated sector’s share in total manufacturing GVA is a mere 13.9 per cent.

Hence, the reason for the GAP must lie in the estimation of organised manufacturing output. The NAS uses company balance-sheet data sourced from the Ministry of Corporate Affairs’ database (MCA-21), compiled using the annual statutory filings by registered companies. This practice of using the MCA data began with the previous NAS revision (base year 2011-12), partially replacing the ASI. The procedure has continued in the latest revision, with minor modifications.

A standard way to validate the GVA is to use employment data to estimate the sector’s potential output by applying appropriate “technical ratios” drawn from the ASI and ASUSE datasets. The official Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) for 2023-24, estimated that the manufacturing sector employed 697.5 lakh workers.

However, as per the ASI and ASUSE datasets, only 532.9 lakh workers were employed to produce the official GVA. Thus, quite possibly, the contribution of the remaining 164.6 lakh “residual workers” — 697.5 minus 532.9 — may account for the GAP in the GVA reported above.

The definitions of employment in the three surveys are not the same, and their data collection methods differ. However, for a validation exercise, the PLFS estimates provide a useful reference point. Official agencies also use similar methods.

Some of this GAP is contributed by the residual 2,72,534 MCA companies, not covered in the 78,618 “private companies” captured in the ASI data. A majority of the residual companies are likely to be to non-factory private companies. The left over residual workers are likely to belong to the unincorporated sector not covered in ASUSE survey because of their small size.

Then, applying the “technical ratios” of the appropriate segments of manufacturing as derived from unit-wise ASI and ASUSE data, the potential GVA of the residual workers is estimated to be ₹3.6 lakh crore.
Then adding the potential GVA to the AE of ₹27.4 lakh crore reported earlier, the likely/potential overall manufacturing GVA could be ₹31.0 lakh crore.

articles.title: Israel elections 2026: Benjamin Netanyahu is down but not out
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Israel’s October 27 election was framed by the Opposition as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu . For the country’s longest-serving Prime Minister, who oversaw the war on Gaza, attacked Iran twice and vowed not to make concessions to Palestinians, the election was a battle for survival. For the Opposition led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, this was an opportunity to oust Mr. Netanyahu from power. With almost 90% of the vote counted, Israel is divided into three blocs, none of which can govern alone.

On the latest count, Mr. Netanyahu’s right-religious coalition has 53 seats, eight short of the 61 needed for a majority in the Knesset. His Likud is the largest party with 26 seats, down from 32 four years ago. His far-right partners, Otzma Yehudit of Ithamar Ben-Gvir (7) and Religious Zionism of Bezalel Smotrich (6), hold 13 between them, down slightly from 14 in the last election. The remaining seats in his bloc come from the religious parties—Shas and United Torah Judaism—each with seven seats.

The Opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, has 48 seats, 13 short of a majority. His Yesh Atid party, which was expected to beat Likud, finished second with 21 seats. His allies, B’Yachad of Naftali Bennett (12) and Israel Beytenu of Avigdor Lieberman (7), add a combined 19. But the main surprise factor of the election was the surge of the Arab parties, which emerged as the third bloc. They have 19 seats between them, with the Joint List winning 12 and the United Arab List (Ra’am) 7.

Likud’s slide is real, but it is smaller than the Opposition had hoped, and Likud outperformed many pre-election polls. Mr. Netanyahu, a wanted man by the International Criminal Court, a divisive figure at home, and the leader of Israel’s right, still commands the single biggest party and the single biggest bloc.

Mr. Netanyahu has built his career on one claim: that only he can “keep Israel safe”. This election was the first test of that claim since the failures of October 7, a war in Gaza that has killed over 70,000 Palestinians, including 20,000 children, and a failed campaign against Iran with global economic consequences. Losing his majority and seeing his party shed seats shows that the claim has weakened, even if it has not collapsed.

But the mechanics of Israeli coalition-building favour the incumbent. Mr. Netanyahu has vowed that he would form a right-wing government. As the leader of the largest party and the largest bloc, Mr. Netanyahu can expect to be invited by President Isaac Herzog to form the government. He will have 24 days to prove the majority. He has two ways forward. First, propose a unity government with Mr. Eisenkot and his allies. But it’s not clear whether Mr. Eisenkot, who has also promised to form the government, would back Mr. Netanyahu as Prime Minister. Second, Mr. Netanyahu could win the support of one of two of Mr. Eisenkot’s right-wing allies (such as Mr. Lieberman or Mr. Bennet) and form a Zionist coalition government. That would break Mr. Eisdenkot’s coalition.

But if Mr. Netanyahu fails to win a majority, the mandate would pass to Mr. Eisenkot, who faces a harder problem. His 48 seats cannot reach 61 without the Arab parties. Even Ra’am’s 7 would take him only to 55. In 2021, Ra’am had supported the Bennet coalition government to keep Mr. Netanyahu out of power. But that experiment collapsed in 2022, forcing the country into another election, which Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition won. The Joint List has always been in opposition, and Mr. Eisdenkot would need their support – either direct or support from outside – to form a government.

This is the Opposition’s central dilemma. Two of Mr. Eisenkot’s allies, Mr. Bennett’s B’Yachard and Mr. Lieberman’s Beytenu, have strongly opposed any alliance with Arab parties. The Opposition campaign was built on ousting Mr. Netanyahu from power, but the opposition coalition needs the support of Arab parties, traditionally kept on the margins of Israel’s power politics, which are reluctant to seek.

If neither bloc gets a majority, Israel would return to the polls within months, with Mr. Netanyahu serving as caretaker Prime Minister throughout. That outcome would suit him. A caretaker government retains the full machinery of the state, and a prolonged campaign would allow him to fall back on his strongest argument — only he can guarantee national security and political stability.

Mr. Netanyahu has lost his majority, his Likud party has shrunk and his claim to be indispensable has been weakened. But the fragmentation of his opponents remains his most reliable asset. He has not won the election, but by denying his opponents an outright victory, he has found a way to cling to power and ensure his political survival, at least for now.

articles.title: U.S. bans imports from Chinese genomics companies over forced labour concerns
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: The United States banned imports from three Chinese genomics companies on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) over claims they collected genetic material used to track persecuted ethnic minorities in China's Xinjiang region.
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said BGI Genomics, MGI Tech and Shenzhen BGI Technology, also known as BGI Group, had been added to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act Entity List.

The list identifies entities working with Xinjiang's government "to recruit, transport, transfer, harbour or receive forced labour or Uyghurs, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, or members of other persecuted groups out of Xinjiang."
The United Nations warned in 2022 of possible crimes against humanity in the region, including the detention of more than a million Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities in camps.
China has repeatedly and vehemently denied accusations of human rights abuses against the Uyghurs.

According to the U.S. DHS, the companies "helped collect genetic material used to track persecuted ethnic minorities, including people subjected to forced labour, meaning work they could not freely refuse."
Beijing said on Thursday (October 29, 2026) that it "strongly condemns" Washington's ban, which has "no factual basis".
"The U.S. side continues to exploit the 'human rights' issue, using it as a pretext to pursue unilateral protectionism and bullying," a Chinese Ministry of Commerce spokesperson said in a statement.
China urged the United States to "immediately cease its political manipulation and smear campaigns", vowing to take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.
Rediscovering Xinjiang: a cultural journey on the ancient Silk Road
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the United States refused to "let companies tied to forced labor and the surveillance of persecuted minorities profit from the American market."
BGI and MGI both denied the allegations, saying they oppose all forms of forced labour.

articles.title: Israel elections: Understanding how Knesset polls work vs India’s system
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Israel faces a high-stakes political standoff after the October 27 national election, the country’s first vote since the 2023 Hamas attack.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his chief rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot of the Yashar party, have both claimed a mandate to form the next government after exit polls showed their respective camps in a neck-and-neck fight without an outright majority, leaving the outcome dependent on the final seat tally and negotiations with smaller parties.

The main difference between Israeli and Indian elections lies in how votes translate into seats. Israel operates under a nationwide system of proportional representation, treating the country as a single voting constituency without separate geographic districts or local MPs. Israelis do not vote for individual candidates. Instead, they cast a single ballot for a closed party list and the 120 seats in parliament, known as the Knesset, are allocated in direct proportion to each party’s share of the national vote.

Meanwhile, India employs a first-past-the-post system (FPTP) across 543 parliamentary constituencies. Indian citizens cast ballots for local candidates in their respective constituencies and whichever candidate secures a majority vote in a constituency wins that seat.

No single political party has ever won an outright 61-seat majority in Israel’s history. With the exit polls on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) too predicting no outright majority for any bloc, forming a coalition government appears to be their only way to go. To enter the 120-seat Knesset, a political list must clear an electoral threshold of 3.25% of the national vote, which equals roughly four seats. Parties that fall short of this line lose all their votes without representation, making party mergers and alliances pertinent ahead of candidate submission deadlines.

For instance, Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition comprises his own right-wing party Likud, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s pro-settler Religious ⁠Zionism and ​National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s far-right Jewish Power.

To form a ruling government in Israel, a coalition must assemble at least 61 seats. This is a requirement that grants small niche factions a disproportionate sway as political kingmakers. If internal divisions cause a minor party to withdraw its support, the entire administration can quickly fall apart. In contrast, Indian political parties frequently build post-poll or pre-poll alliances. Additionally, major national parties in India can and often do win single-party majority mandates without relying on minor regional partners for survival.

In India, the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party secured outright single-party majority in back-to-back general elections, winning 282 seats in 2014 and 303 seats in 2019, well above the 272-seat majority mark in the 543-member Lok Sabha. But in the 2024 general elections, the PM Modi-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) bagged only 286 seats, with the BJP winning 240 seats and falling 32 short of the majority mark of 272 seats, prompting a coalition with their allies.

After the official results are published, Israel President Isaac Herzog will consult representatives of the elected parliamentary factions before assigning a lawmaker the task of forming a government.
The President generally selects the candidate considered best placed to secure parliamentary support, rather than being required to choose the leader of the largest party.

The first nominee has 28 days to form a government, with the President able to grant extensions of up to 14 additional days. If the attempt fails, another lawmaker may be given an opportunity. If subsequent efforts also fail, the process could lead to another election.

articles.title: Afghanistan opium poppy cultivation surges despite Taliban government ban: UN
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Opium poppy cultivation in Afghanistan more than quadrupled in 2026 despite a Taliban government ban, the United Nations said Thursday (October 29, 2026), urging that impoverished farmers needed alternatives to the lucrative crop.

Cultivated areas reached 43,000 hectares (around 1,06,200 acres), up from 10,000 hectares in 2025, while estimated opium production jumped fivefold from 300 tonnes to 1,500 tonnes, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) said in a report.

Long the world’s leading producer of poppies, Afghanistan was overtaken by Myanmar after a 2022 Taliban government ban crushed the trade in the country. But rampant poverty has driven some farmers to return to the trade.
“Without opium, we cannot even afford basic food,” Mohammad, a 22-year-old farmer in Afghanistan’s northeast, told AFP .
Afghanistan’s 2022 crackdown drove cultivated areas down from more than 2,00,000 hectares to 10,000 hectares in 2025.
Myanmar cultivated 53,000 hectares in 2025, with no 2026 figures available. The Taliban authorities claim to have destroyed more than 22,000 hectares.
But UNODC said many poppy plots were concealed among cereal crops or behind walls, making them difficult to detect.
Mr. Mohammad lives with his parents in Badakhshan which has become Afghanistan’s main opium poppy-growing province.
“The Taliban threaten us and do not allow us to grow opium. We cultivate it with a great deal of fear,” he said, asking only to be identified by his first name.
“I want to buy a car, build a house and get married. Without opium, I cannot achieve these things,” he further explained.
In May, two people were killed in clashes that erupted as Afghan security forces moved to destroy opium poppy fields in Badakhshan.

Another 35-year-old farmer named Mohammad, who ploughs his poppy field with an ox, said: “If we grow wheat, it is not enough to sustain our lives. We are forced to grow poppies to earn a good income.”

articles.title: India ready to share 'battle-tested' anti-terror expertise with ASEAN, its dialogue partners: Rajnath Singh
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: India is ready to share its "battle-tested" counter-terror expertise with ASEAN and its dialogue partners, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said on Thursday (October 29, 2026) as he described Operation Sindoor as a declaration of New Delhi's clear approach against state-sponsored terrorist activities.
The Defence Minister also said that India supports an Indo-Pacific that is secure and resilient -- one where peace and stability are not merely aspirations, but the outcome of collective efforts.

In an address at a conclave of defence ministers of ASEAN member states and the bloc's dialogue partners in Cebu in the Philippines, he flagged concerns over disruptions in certain maritime trade routes and asserted that India will continue to act as a "trusted net security provider" in the Indian Ocean region and the wider Indo-Pacific.

"Today, when global trade routes are facing new types of international threats, merely issuing statements on maritime security is not enough," he said at the ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting Plus (ADMM-Plus) conclave.

However, what drew more attention was Mr. Singh's call for concerted efforts to combat terrorism. "India is fully prepared to share its practical and battle-tested counter-terrorism expertise with ADMM-Plus partners," he said.
"Through joint military exercises, capacity-building programmes, and robust intelligence sharing, we can further strengthen our collective capabilities," he added.

The Defence Minister said that a major example of India's approach against terrorism was last year's Operation Sindoor when a large number of terrorist infrastructures were destroyed. "This was also a declaration of India's clear approach against state-sponsored terror," he said.

India's experience in the field of counter-terrorism is not just classroom or theoretical knowledge, but rather an experience gained over decades while confronting cross-border security challenges, he said, referring to Pakistan's use of terrorism against India.
"Every strategy of ours against terrorism has been tested and proven in actual operations and has demonstrated its success," he said.

Mr. Singh also outlined India's vision for the Indo-Pacific. "We support an Indo-Pacific that is secure and resilient -- one where peace and stability are not merely aspirations, but the outcome of our collective efforts," he said.

He said India considers maritime security to be an issue connected to peace, security, and prosperity in the region. "India's emphasis on the rule of law, and particularly on the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), as well as its advocacy for freedom of navigation and overflight, is not against any country. Rather, its purpose is to protect the collective interests of all regional stakeholders," he said.

Mr. Singh’s remarks came amid consistent demands by several ASEAN member states as well as democratic nations for adherence to UNCLOS in the face of Beijing's increasing military muscle flexing in the contested South China Sea.

articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The story so far: Microsoft has introduced a voluntary exit offer for eligible employees in India , the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, as the technology giant expands its artificial intelligence (AI) business and changes how work is organised.

In an October 26 announcement, Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s executive vice-president and chief people officer, said the offer would give eligible employees considering leaving the company financial support and career-planning resources. The programme is available to employees in selected teams, with participation depending on business priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs.

The latest offer follows two earlier workforce measures, such as the elimination of around 4,800 roles and a Voluntary Retirement Program in which more than 30% of eligible employees chose to participate. Microsoft has not disclosed how many employees it expects to leave under the new offer.

While the company has not explicitly linked the latest programme to AI-driven job displacement or cost savings, its workforce announcements, financial disclosures and account of its internal AI transformation provide context for the decision.

Microsoft is restructuring even as its business grows. In its fiscal 2026 results, the company reported revenue of $331.8 billion, up 18% from the previous year, and operating income of $155.2 billion, up 21%.

Kamal Karanth, co-founder of specialist staffing firm Xpheno, described Microsoft’s voluntary exit offer (VEO) as “a timely manpower optimisation move” against the backdrop of operational efficiencies achieved over the last four fiscal periods.
He said enterprises strive for “non-linear scale and growth on manpower to revenue ratios”, and Microsoft appears to have achieved this over the last four years.

According to the four-year comparison he shared, Microsoft’s revenue grew 79.7% and its headcount rose 68.7% between FY2018 and FY2022. Between FY2022 and FY2026, revenue grew 67.4%, while headcount increased just 0.9%.
“Achieving a 68% growth in revenue with less than 1% net growth in headcount over the last 4 fiscals, denotes an operational excellence in play,” he said.

Mr. Karanth said Microsoft had got several things right, including its “product and revenue mix, client mix, quality and pedigree of talent, AI tech stack impact on productivity, and efficiency of Cloud and AI infrastructure”.

Comparing the two periods, he described the shift as “a successful switch up to non-linear scale and efficiency”. He said the efficiencies achieved so far provided “sufficient headroom for the company to slim down, optimise headcounts and improve output efficiencies as AI matures further”.

In a July 6 announcement about job cuts, Ms. Coleman said the company was eliminating around 4,800 roles, about 2.1% of its global workforce, as it aligned its workforce and investments with changing business priorities.

articles.title: Experts in stroke medicine emphasise on timely treatment
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Chennai-based stroke medicine expert Sivarajan Thandeswaran has called for certification of Indian hospitals to distinguish them as ‘stroke-ready’ so that people do not waste time in seeking treatment.

“Hospitals in India have to apply for and obtain NABH or JCI certification; instead, a proper government legislation making it mandatory for patients to be taken to and treated at comprehensive stroke centres, as done in the West, will improve stroke care,” said a senior consultant in Stroke Medicine, General Internal Medicine and Gerontology, at Kauvery Hospital in Alwarpet on Wednesday.

He was speaking at a webinar on ‘The Golden Hour: Every Minute Matters, Every Life Counts’, presented by Kauvery Hospital in association with The Hindu to mark World Stroke Day, observed annually on October 29.

He was joined by Harish R. Kamath, consultant neurologist, Kauvery Hosur. The experts stressed on the need for timely access to care as time is the most crucial factor to salvage the brain. Stroke is the second leading cause of death and, therefore, treatment in the window period of 4.5 hours is critical.
Treatment of stroke has transformed tremendously, and families need to be aware, Dr. Thandeswaran added.

In his presentation, Dr. Kamath explained the symptoms of stroke, including loss of balance, blurring vision, facial asymmetry, weakness in arms, and slurring speech. He said 1.8 million new stroke cases are added every year and 7.25 million deaths due to stroke occur every year.

Dr. Thandeswaran said that while big city hospitals have facilities for scanning, imaging, and treatment, including thrombolysis (dissolving blood clots with medicine) and thrombectomy (removing clot through surgery), in remote areas, telemedicine and video calls were being used in identifying stroke patients and transferring them to Comprehensive Stroke Centres, where advanced services and specialist teams are available.
The doctors discussed lifestyle-related risks, including poor dietary habits, physical inactivity, and inadequate sleep.
“People should take ownership of their health through routine check-ups for better treatment outcomes,” Dr. Thandeswaran suggested.

articles.title: Why India rejected a patent application for shorter drug-resistant TB treatment | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The story so far: The Indian Patent Office has rejected a patent application filed by the U.S.-based Global Alliance for TB Drug Development (TB Alliance) for the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid, known as BPaL. The six-month, all-oral regimen is recommended by the World Health Organisation (WHO) for eligible patients with certain forms of drug-resistant tuberculosis.

BPaL — bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid — provides a shorter, more effective treatment for people with highly drug-resistant tuberculosis, for whom older regimens could involve 18–24 months of treatment, multiple medicines and, in some cases, painful injections.

The development is also central to the debate over intellectual property and access to medicines, because the treatment combines existing drugs with pretomanid, a newer anti-TB medicine developed by the non-profit TB Alliance.

India’s recent decision to reject the patent application follows two pre-grant oppositions filed in 2020. One was filed by Eldred Tellis of Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust and Ganesh Acharya, with support from the Lawyers’ Collective and the Médecins Sans Frontières Access Campaign. The other was filed by the Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), with support from the Third World Network (TWN).

The organisations have now welcomed the decision, arguing that the application sought patent protection for a combination of medicines and a treatment approach already disclosed in earlier scientific research and clinical trials.
“India’s latest decision will help facilitate generic competition and improve access to treatment,’’ said the group.

At the core of the dispute is the question — whether combining three existing medicines into a treatment regimen qualifies for a new patent. Health experts in their statement noted that research and clinical trials dating back to 2015 had already disclosed the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid, as well as its use in a shorter treatment course. They noted that the application now did not establish an inventive step sufficient to justify granting a new monopoly and patent.

Their challenge invoked three provisions of India’s Patents Act. Section 3(d) restricts patents on certain new forms or uses of known substances that do not demonstrate the required enhancement in efficacy. Section 3(e) excludes substances that do not result in enhanced efficacy. Section 3(i) excludes methods of medical treatment from patentability.
The opponents also argued that the application did not sufficiently disclose the claimed invention. Patent Office upheld all grounds of opposition.

India continues to carry the world’s largest tuberculosis burden. According to the WHO’s Global Tuberculosis Report 2025, an estimated 2.71 million people developed TB in India in 2024, accounting for about 25% of global cases. The estimated incidence rate was 187 cases per 100,000 people.

Drug-resistant TB adds to the challenge because the disease can require specialised treatment, careful monitoring and prolonged engagement with health services. High treatment costs can place pressure on households, particularly when illness affects a person’s ability to work and earn an income.

India’s national TB programme provides free diagnosis and treatment through public health services. However, access to medicines alone does not resolve all the challenges faced by patients, including treatment-related adverse effects, loss of income, travel costs and the need for nutritional and social support.

articles.title: Taxonomic ‘chauvinism’ rife in ecological literature
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The ‘blockbuster’ drug, Ozempic, was created with the help of a most unlikely source: the saliva of a humble lizard. And spiders and scorpions have led to the development of life-saving medicines. But, of the 1.5 million animal species known to live on planet Earth (with many more yet to be discovered), just a fraction of them — mainly vertebrates — monopolise scientific research and literary attention, undermining scientific breakthroughs, find two new studies.

Scientists from the University of New South Wales, Australia (UNSW) sifted through 1,383,803 research papers worldwide on ecology and evolution and found, for instance, that even though birds and mammals comprise less than 1 per cent of animal biodiversity, they dominate both conservation and research efforts. The studies were published in the journal Ecology and Evolution here and here. They added that vertebrates appear in 53.9 per cent of all papers in this field, although they represent only 4.7 per cent of animal biodiversity

On the other hand, the authors discovered that species-rich invertebrate groups, such as arachnids and insects “are often relegated to taxonomically specialised journals, which probably reach a narrower audience.” This strong taxonomic bias, or ‘taxonomical chauvinism’ (disproportionate attention given to some taxa relative to their diversity) was found across papers on ecology and evolution.

“We also observed that studies on vertebrates, relative to those on invertebrates, were more prevalent in higher impact journals and, within journals, received more citations and mentions in the media,” wrote the authors. Sometimes invertebrates such as parasites sneak in to the literature, but “only… because of their association with vertebrates.”
The studies go on to untangle this bias, and ponder over the factors that could shape an ecologist’s or evolutionary biologist’s choices of the organisms they study.

One reason, they said could be attributed to mundane factors such as the logistical ease of study, or societal relevance, especially when it came to major animal groups. Next, they could be linked to the prominence of certain organisms within peer networks “or early-career exposure to specific taxa.”

Finally “emotional factors” could shape the choice of research, including taxonomic affinities: for instance, the movie Finding Nemo , “ is an example of how culture can influence people’s perception of nature and encourage people to pursue a scientific career,” lead author Pietro Pollo, from UNSW Science told The Hindu .

Even zoos everywhere in the world are usually filled with big mammals, so people know what a lion or a giraffe is, but they rarely know much about the animals living near them (especially invertebrates). The researchers found evidence that people study animals they are “fond of”: those they think are pretty, cute, interesting, or fascinating, showing how the cultural factors that we are all exposed to can influence scientists’ decisions, Dr. Pollo added.

The bias doesn’t just stop at scientific literature: it goes beyond, to grants awarded, biodiversity databases, conservation or reintroduction projects and textbooks. “For example, vertebrates, especially birds and mammals, often concentrate conservation and research efforts even though they represent only a minute portion of existing animals,” said a paper.

This scientific “hyperfocus” on certain organisms slows innovation: “We should diversify our research as much as we can, casting a wider net to increase our chances of ‘winning the jackpot’,” said Dr. Pollo.

Divya Uma, a biology professor at Azim Premji University, concurred with these findings. “Since humans are visual creatures, the attention, even in popular media, focusses more on larger, charismatic mammals,” she told The Hindu . She added that indeed, any subject that affects humans immediately or directly “is perceived to be important,”: for instance, research on human health and diseases gets more funding worldwide.

The authors of the UNSW papers propose a series of targeted actions to ameliorate taxonomic imbalances in ecology and evolution, such as outreach initiatives featuring neglected taxa, taxonomically equitable education and taxonomically diverse research experiences. This inequity, can after all, “stifle innovation in medicine and engineering,” they added.
